context.text: On January 23, 2020 China locked down Wuhan, a city of 11 million, and soon extended restrictions to the surrounding province. It was the first sign of how seriously Beijing viewed the outbreak, coming on the eve of the Lunar New Year holiday.
context.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code)

analysis.text: China reacted first: the Hang Seng fell 7% in the first week, with Chinese energy, metals and auto stocks each down about 12%. The US barely moved, down 1.1%, and US autos even gained. Energy fell in all three markets as investors expected lower fuel demand. The three-month losses of 15-21% reflect the virus's spread to the rest of the world, not the lockdown alone.

headlines.abstract: A rout that began in Asia continued in Europe, and U.S. stocks are set to fall sharply. Japan’s benchmark index logged its worst single-day point decline.

context.text: On August 5, 2024 Japan's Nikkei fell more than 12%, its worst day since 1987, after a Bank of Japan rate rise and weak US jobs data pushed the yen higher and forced investors to unwind trades funded in yen. Volatility spiked worldwide.
context.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code)

analysis.text: Measured from the previous Friday's close, after losses had already begun, the shock was short-lived: the S&P 500 was flat after a week and up 3.4% after a month. Sector moves were small in the first week, all within about 3 points of their markets. Chinese sectors rose strongly over three months, but that reflects Beijing's stimulus in late September. Japanese stocks, which took the biggest hit, are not covered here.

headlines.title: China plays down devaluation fears as yuan cut for third straight day

context.text: On August 11, 2015 the People's Bank of China cut the yuan's daily reference rate by nearly 2%, its biggest move in two decades, and said the rate would follow the market more closely. Investors read it as a sign that China's economy was weaker than it looked and feared a currency war.
context.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code)

analysis.text: Chinese tech fell 10.6% in a week, lagging the Hang Seng by 6 points, and European autos fell 8%, lagging their market by 5.5 points. European carmakers sell many cars in China, so a weaker yuan and slowing demand hit them directly, while US automakers rose. Within a month all three markets were down 7-12%, a window that includes the global sell-off of August 24. Chinese autos rose 26% over three months, which more likely reflects China's car purchase tax cut announced in late September.
analysis.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code)
